title: Visualization:  Hierarchical Navigable Small World
tagline: Watch vector search find its answer in real time
pitch: An interactive 3D visualization of FAISS's HNSW algorithm that shows exactly how a nearest-neighbor search moves through graph layers to find a result.
description: An interactive 3D visualization that makes FAISS's HNSW search algorithm easy to see and understand. I forked and recompiled FAISS to record every node visited during a search, built a Python/Flask pipeline to generate embeddings and HNSW indexes over Gutenberg and Wikipedia datasets, and used PCA/UMAP to project them into 3D. The React and Three.js frontend lets users run real text searches and watch the query traverse graph layers toward its result.

caseStudy.problem: HNSW is the algorithm behind most modern vector search, but it's usually explained with static diagrams of graph layers. Those diagrams don't show how a single query moves through the structure to reach its nearest neighbors.
caseStudy.approach: I built a Flask pipeline that generates sentence embeddings and full HNSW indexes over the Gutenberg and Wikipedia datasets, then used PCA and UMAP to project those high-dimensional embeddings down to 3D coordinates. A React and Three.js frontend renders the resulting graph, so a real text query can be typed in and watched as it moves toward its answer.
caseStudy.challenge: FAISS doesn't expose what happens inside a search, so getting a real traversal path meant going into its C++ HNSW implementation directly. I forked the library, dug through the search code, and added logic to record every node it visited and which layer each one belonged to. After recompiling FAISS with those changes, I ran searches against the modified build, which is what made it possible to show an actual search path through the graph instead of a simulated one.
caseStudy.result: The final tool lets anyone type a search, watch the algorithm drop into the top layer and narrow down through each level, and see the visited path highlighted against the full graph. It's the visualization I wanted when I was first learning how vector search worked.
caseStudy.learned: Let users compare two queries side by side to see how their search paths diverge, and expose graph parameters like M and efSearch so people can see how they change the shape of the graph.
